Mr. Karic directly witnessed the beatings of other prisoners. Three prisoners, Smail Pandzic, Alija Jusufovic and Nasko Smajic, were, in particular, regularly targeted and beaten. At the beginning of July, all three were beaten to death by Rajko Kusic's men. When Malko Koroman, the chief of police in Pale, came to the prison and saw the dead body of one of those men, he remarked, "There must be some kind of plague in the prison." Mr. Karic and 33 other detainees were moved to Kula Prison on 11 July. The accused visited Kula Prison on one occasion while Mr. Karic was there. Mr. Karic was exchanged on the 28th of August, 1992. That concludes the summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, I have just a handful of further questions for you. You referred to the fact, in your statement, that detainees were routinely called out of the room where you were detained, and that this occurred to you on the 28th of June, 1992. Can you describe for the Court what happened when you were called out of the room on this date?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: On that day, they took me out to a smaller room that was in front of the hall. It was in concrete --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, the interpreters couldn't hear you, the last, but could you repeat your answer, please, and speak to the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I walked into a smaller room that was in front of the hall that was all in concrete, and there was a piece of gym equipment there. Two Serbian soldiers met me there, and they held sticks in their hands. They started beating me straight away for 10 or 15 minutes, while I was still standing on my feet. They were beating me on the back, on the head, and then I fell on the right side. And then I received quite a few blows on the left side, on my shoulder, back and head. Then I passed out. I just heard someone walk in, Milomir Tepes [Realtime transcript read in error "Tepic"]. He worked at the sawmill, and he said, No, it's not him, he's not the one. Then they stopped beating me, and somehow they managed to get me up on my feet and throw me back into the hall where the other detainees were. My left arm was all black, and I lay there helpless for days without any help. That was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: In your statement, Mr. Karic, and we've just heard it in the summary of your statement, you say Malko Koroman, the chief of police, came to the centre where you were being detained, and he said something like, There must be some kind of plague in the prison. How do you know he said that?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: A few days after we were beaten - there were several of us who had been beaten - I described that in my statements about these three men who died. Actually, two of them died on the same day, and the third one died two days later. Malko Koroman entered the hall one day and said, somewhat surprised, What is this, as if I have some kind of plague here. I have to transfer you from here to somewhere else, but the conditions were not good. That was it. But that did not happen. He did not transfer us anywhere else. We still stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: What did he see in front of him that appeared to prompt this statement from him? Can you describe the scene he saw?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Well, he saw these men who were lying there. Actually, this one young man who was lying down on the floor, it was as if his brains had oozed out on the floor. And then he said, Is this the plague or what? We, the prisoners, were lying down. We couldn't stand on our feet because we were being beaten every day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And, finally, with respect to that: Judging from the circumstances, did it appear he really thought there was some kind of plague in this prison?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Oh no, he did not. He was sort of trying to justify himself, pretending not to know anything about it. I don't know how to explain this to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: In your statement, you say that around 11 of July, you were moved to Kula Prison. And you describe your detention at Kula, and you state that there were also women and children detained there. How did you learn that women and children were being detained while you were there?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Well, the men who were there with me found out by way of mirrors. They were talking with this other room by way of the mirror, Where are you from? These were civilians from Hadzici, women, children. There were also some men there as well. They were brought there from their houses. So it's not that there were imprisoned soldiers there. It was all civilians who were brought from our homes, just as we were brought from our homes as civilians, not as any kind of military.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: You say that you found out or men you were being detained with by way of mirrors. Can you just explain to the Court exactly how they used mirrors to find out this information?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Well, you take a mirror out this way [indicates], and then you'd turn it towards the other room, and then people would look at each other and talk. Some people could get their heads out a bit and they could talk, sort of.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: While you were at Kula, did any of the detainees perform work?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Yes, work was performed, trenches were dug. Some people went to bury the dead, and others went to the farm to work there, to dig, to work at the chicken farm, to put the eggs away, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And why did these detainees perform this work?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Well, they made them go every day. Some went to dig trenches. Others went to bury the dead. The greatest problem was burying the dead, because these bodies were decaying, I think, and they had to be buried. As they were going back, these people were vomiting. They would be sick for 10 days or whatever. They went there mostly for food, because if they went out to dig, then they were given some food. The soldiers from the front-line would give them something, or some of the locals there, things like that. And that is why they had to go, basically, because that was a way to survive, because the food was very bad. I don't know if I described this anywhere, but while I was in Pale, I got only a slice of bread and a bit of water over 24 hours. So on the 28th of May, when I was taken prisoner, up until the 11th of July, I would only get a slice of bread and a bit of water, whereas in Kula I had sort of a slice of bread and some kind of soup which wasn't greasy, or salty, or anything. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Finally, with respect to Kula, you discuss a visit by Mr. Karadzic in August, and I want to show you a film clip relating to a visit by Mr. Karadzic. Before that is shown, let me ask you some questions. At the time of the visit, was the normal routine of the prison followed by the detainees?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: That day when we heard that Karadzic would come to visit with I don't know who else, before they came, it wasn't really that clean. The food and so on, that day, they kind of fixed it up to be a bit nice. They didn't let us go out, but they let us go out a little bit then. While I was in Pale, the first time I went out was on the 28th. That was the first time I went out in the period from the 28th of May until the 11th of July. We were shut up. I was ill. We were not permitted to go out anywhere. I felt dizzy. I had lost weight. I had lost 50 kilos, not 10 kilos. I lost 50 kilos. I kept falling to the side. I was unable to walk, so I didn't really go out for work much, until one day one of those guys there asked me, Why don't you go out? And I was quiet, and somebody said, He cannot work, he's sick. And that's when some man came to me. After then, he took me to the infirmary. Actually, he was taking me somewhere, I wasn't sure where he was taking me. And then when I entered that room, I could see that it was some kind of infirmary, there were medicines there. He said he wanted to help me, to examine me. I took my top off. My arm was all black, it was stiff. I couldn't move it. He gave me some balm, he put something on it, and then he took me back to the room before Karadzic came. So it wasn't like that. They kind of camouflaged it, they fixed it up a little bit, so it didn't look like they were mistreating us, like it was bad. They wanted to make it look like they were taking care of us, but it was only like that for that one day while Dr. Karadzic was making the tour with the journalists and the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And just to clarify, Mr. Karic, the visit to the infirmary, did that occur at Kula or Pale?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: In Kula, in Kula.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I'd now like to play 65 ter 40173A in Sanction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We need to switch to Sanction? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: If we could pause, please. We should be receiving sound for this video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The technicians will take a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: We may be able to view it without the sound. If we admit it into evidence with the sound, and we can deal with it on that basis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wonder if we -- could we have interpretations of the captions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do we have it, Mr. Hayden?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Well, the sound is being interpreted by the captions, Mr. President. So if we had sound, everyone would be able to follow along in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: But could the interpreters interpret the captions as we're looking at it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We believe that it might be a little bit too fast for us to do it without a transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I'm happy to proceed. The interpreters have indicated they're unable to translate that. The parties can view this with sound, because it will be admitted into evidence with the sound. And perhaps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How long will this clip be?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: It's approximately 2 minutes and 10 seconds, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's do it without sound.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: " ... get a few cigarettes from their visitors. "'The conditions are good here,' says this man -- "

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So we can start again. You turned down the volume. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: "Reporter: 57 Muslims were being held at this Serb-run prison, the date of our visit. Most are between the age of 20 and 60, and all those we saw appear to be in fairly good shape, grateful to get a few cigarettes from their visitors. The conditions are good here, says this man. Everyone we asked said the same thing, although a few did look desperately thin. Indeed, Kula, on the outskirts of Sarajevo, has been a prison for the last 20 years, and it is not on the list of detention centres that outsider services have requested to see. Yet this is where the first international observer has been brought. He is Paddy Ashdown, leader of Britain's Liberal Democrat Party. He was invited by the president of the Bosnian Serbs, Radovan Karadzic, under great pressure since reports of Serbian concentration camps made world headlines. Karadzic made a great show of standing aside while Ashdown interviewed these prisoners." "Ashdown: There's never been any concern about the way this particular camp is run, but I want to suspend my judgement until I see some of the other camps." "Reporter: And Karadzic chose this moment to make his first so-called unilateral gesture of international goodwill, releasing just ten prisoners, those who are over 60 or in poor health. Smiling, he handed out release papers as though he was handing out awards, and it brought tears of joy to those who were being freed. "The Serbs say they hold a maximum of 8.250 prisoners, not the 58.000 that the opposition claimed. They say they'd like to get rid of all of them, but, say the Serbs, they've had no reciprocal gestures by the Muslims and Croats." "Karadzic: We released only people who are not likely to be mobilised again. If we released all of those people without exchange, they would be mobilised immediately and they would fight against us. It would be unreasonable." "Reporter: The Serbs say all the people here are fighters. The prisoners say they are not." "I don't know weapons. I didn't shoot." "Reporter: This man is blind in one eye. He says he couldn't fight even if he wanted to. They all say they've been taken as bargaining chips traded for prisoners from the other side, and they don't expect to be released anytime soon. "Christiane Amanpour, at Kula Prison outside Sarajevo."

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, is that the visit by Mr. Karadzic that you refer to in your statement?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: We saw, at the end of that clip, Mr. Karadzic stating that he would release those who -- he would not release those who are likely to be mobilised again. When you were arrested, Mr. Karic, were you a member of the military or a member of an armed group?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: I wasn't a member of any group, and I was not armed. I wasn't a member of any party at the time. I didn't have any weapons or anything like that. They came to my house -- actually, to my cousin's house. They took me away, saying they were looking for me at the MUP to provide some sort of a statement. But they actually just locked me up.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And from your conversations with the other detainees at Pale and in Kula, were you aware of other detainees who were not members of the military or any armed group?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Everyone who was with me in Pale, none of them were from any armed group, from any front. They were from homes. When there was an attack in Renovica, they assembled people from houses, whatever they could. They put them together, brought them to Pale. These people were not on front-lines, not in any kind of combat. They actually just rounded up the civilians and brought them in. And there were all these other people from Grahovo, and this guy, Nasko Smajic from Majdan, and these others, all of them, as far as I know, were not at the front. They were civilians, who were brought in, rounded up and arrested from their homes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: I tender that clip into evidence. And that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: They will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P2840, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: And no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Karic, you'll be further asked by Mr. Karadzic, as part of his cross-examination. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Good day, Mr. Karic.

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You got your consolidated statement that you certified and signed on the 10th of May, 2011; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The two of us, since we're speaking the same language, we will have to make pauses. So I kindly ask you to understand why I am waiting. Did you get that statement in your own language then?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And did you ask that it be in your language or did they give it to you without you having to ask for it?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask for anything. Well, it's quite normal for them to give it to me in my own language to read it, because I wouldn't be able to understand it in any other language.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement, paragraph 4, we say that everything began on the 1st of March, 1992. Paragraph 4, if you have the statement, can you please look at that paragraph. I think the referendum was held on the 1st of March, that's when it all began. Is that something that you link with the referendum?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: The referendum was held on the 1st of March. Already on the 2nd of March, it was a little bit of a strange time. It was not possible to move around normally. It was a little bit -- well, it wasn't normal. That day, I went to work, and some strange things were going on. And after all of that, it wasn't a normal situation. It was kind of tense, as if something were being expected for something to happen, although I didn't believe that. But it did happen, something ugly did happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Are you thinking of some particular dramatic event in Sarajevo on the 1st of March?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not thinking of any particular dramatic event, but it was the sense that I had. There was no freedom of speech, talking. The situation was tense. It wasn't normal. I don't know how I could describe it. It wasn't the way it was before usually. Something strange was happening. In Pale, for example, next to my business unit where I was working, there was the firefighting brigade, and one day I could see armed people who were coming and going in trucks. They were being taken to Trebevic, up there. That's what I heard. That was my first bad impression, what is going on. I asked myself something is wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. We'll come back to that. Let me remind you, then. On the 1st of March, didn't Celo, in Bascarsija, fire at a Serbian wedding procession and kill the bridegroom's father?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: I only heard something about that, a little bit. I really didn't pay attention to that. I wasn't watching the news. There was a little bit of talk about that, but I didn't really pay that much attention to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did he kill him a little bit or did he kill him outright?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I'm saying I didn't really give it that much attention. It wasn't something that I was interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What about the barricades and obstacles on the roads and these strange events? Are you not connecting them to that strange incident?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that the barricades were erected in the evening, after that killing, and that they stayed there on the 2nd of March too?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: I didn't notice that. I didn't notice any barricades, even though I was commuting to work and back. I went to work as usual on the 2nd of March and other days. I didn't notice anything, I didn't notice any barricades.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 6, you say that you saw a large gathering of Serbs in Pale. Are you connecting that gathering with the killing of Nikola Basevic in Bascarsija next to the Serbian Orthodox church?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't make any connections between those events, because I don't know anything about the incident anyway. I just had the idea that because of the referendum, and after that something seemed to be up, something was strange, about to happen. I wasn't a member of any party, so I didn't really believe that anything really would happen. Had I believed that something would happen, I wouldn't have gone to Pale to work on the day that I did, had I believed that there would be something happening or that war would break out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, to make it easier for the Trial Chamber to understand, is it correct that you worked in Sarajevo -- you lived in Sarajevo and worked at Pale, which is some 15 kilometres away, even though it was still a city municipality?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's true, I worked from 1984 in Pale, when that work unit was opened there, until the war broke out in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 7, you are describing the 4th of April, 1992. You say that you set out for work. You had to pass through several check-points. Was there a Muslim check-point near the Vijecnica exit in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And were you allowed to pass through? Were you checked? Were you asked anything when you were allowed to pass through?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Well, I came through with a van, minivan. They stopped at the Vijecnica, picked me up. The van was stopped, it was checked, and then it was allowed to pass.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then you encountered a Serbian check-point near the tunnel; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Yes, at Kozja Cuprija.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You passed two check-points on your way to Pale. Can you please tell us what happened at those check-points? Can you please tell us what happened?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Well, it was just that one check-point at Kozja Cuprija where there was Serb soldiers. There was a professor among them from Pale. I don't remember his name right now. All the others were familiar to me as well. They were in uniforms. Their faces were blackened a little bit. They were just looking a little bit, checking our papers, and they let us through.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And what was your means of transport?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: It was Opres [as interpreted] van, the van that transported newspaper to Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Allow me to read paragraph 7 of your statement.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We do not have the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: "I set off for work on such and such a day, and on the way I had to pass through several check-points. At the first check-point, near the second tunnel towards Pale, there was the regular police. They looked at the car, and then they allowed me to pass through. The second check-point was at Kozja Cuprija. It was manned by the reserve police of Pale. They wore the blue, thick uniform of the reserve police. I was allowed to pass without difficulties." Let us clarify this now. Were you going with your own car, you say they checked the car, or were you going by van?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: I don't know how it's written here. I said that I was going by van. I did not have my own car at the time. I didn't have my own car, and I wasn't a driver. And I actually think that is a little bit relevant, whether I went with my own car or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The Defence thinks it's important. They would like the statement to be correct and precise. I don't want to be splitting hairs here. And, forgive me, but I would like to see exactly what happened. Were your IDs checked on these roads?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Was it the police or the army?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: The police was at the first check-point. Up there, it was the reserve police. And I mentioned that professor over there. He wasn't in the police; he was a professor at school. But on that day, he was in a multi-coloured uniform at the check-point. There were several others there also wearing camouflage uniforms at Kozja Cuprija.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us see what you said in your statement from 1992. Can we look at 1D3675 in the e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: We're yet to be notified of any cross-examination documents for this witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope that the e-mail went out, but this was after the solemn statement given by -- solemn oath given by Mr. Karic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think it hasn't. Let's proceed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you see this second paragraph: "During this second control, I recognised Policeman Furtula, who told me that Centrotrans' bus on the Pale-Sarajevo route was stopped, and the passengers were robbed, the driver beaten, and his pistol was taken. He also told me that I probably would not be able to return to Sarajevo that day." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: This statement here is correct, but it was a long time ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Who stopped the bus, and who was the driver?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: It was Lazar Bojat who was driving.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A Serb; right?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Yes, from Pale. He was driving on the Renovica-Sarajevo route.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Who stopped and robbed them and beat him up?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: According to what he said, he said it was at the first barricades from Sarajevo. Allegedly, he's saying that the passengers were robbed. They said that they found a pistol in his waistband, and they allegedly struck him on the head with that pistol, and then they returned him back with all the passengers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did they hit him or did they beat him up so that he had to seek treatment?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: No, they just hit him on the head. I saw him there when he came to Pale, I mean, I saw him. It was nothing. They had hit him on the head with a pistol, but it wasn't really anything much that you could see.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Could we now see in e-court 65 ter -- excuse me, 1D802, and this the same as 65 ter 3718. 1D802, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you look at this and also allow us to see how the press agency reported about this: "A bus driver on the Renovica-Sarajevo route, Lazar Bojat, on Sunday, the 5th of April, 1992, replaced his Muslim colleague so that he could celebrate the Muslim holiday of Bajram. "In front of the underpass in Sarajevo which leads to the transit road, Bojat and his bus full of passengers were stopped by traps set up along the road. Immediately after they were stopped, the bus was shot at from the tunnel with automatic weapons. Uniformed persons which were wearing red berets forced the driver to drive the bus between the traps into the tunnel in which some 50 Red Berets and one police car were located." Do you see that? And then you can see that they took 120.000 from the conductor, they beat and harassed the passengers, and the bus driver was beaten over the head by the Red Berets with is own gun for which he had a permit. "After this mistreatment, the passengers were forced to walk to Sarajevo, and two members of the Red Berets drove the bus off. "Bojat arrived with the passengers to the City Hall and said that he recognised those same Red Berets in the car with the insignia of the United Nations." Is this that event?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is that event, but I think that there are a lot of additions here. I don't know who gave the statement, it was probably the driver, and he stated what he saw, half of it is not true.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. The witness has given his version of events. He's stated that half of this is not true, and doesn't confirm its contents in that respect.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I believe that half would be enough, anyway, the half that he confirmed as being true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: With that comment of the witness's, we can admit this. That all goes to the probative value or weight of the evidence. We'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1400, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So Furtula informed you that perhaps you wouldn't be able to come back because the bus was not running; right?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Well, sort of right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Taken away; right?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Who?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, the bus that was supposed to take you again from Pale to Sarajevo. It was taken away, the Red Berets took it away; right?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Well, how did the driver return to Pale again if it was taken away; the bus, I mean? Why don't you explain that to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It says here that he came with the passengers on foot to town hall; that is to say, that he returns in some different way.

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: He could only return on that bus, and that was the last thing. Nothing else managed to get through. This bus was returned, and never again did anything go either this way or that way. Had it been possible, I would have gone back.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Furtula knew you; right?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And he said that there was no bus, that that was the reason why you couldn't go back, not because you were a Muslim; right?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether he put it that way. I don't remember that. I -- I mean, he just said, Well, just see what's happening there. He didn't say anything else. Since he knew that I was the boss of those drivers, he told me of this happening, and that was it. When I came to Pale, I found Lazar there, and that is to say the bus and him and everything, so it wasn't that the bus was taken away. I don't know why he gave this statement that it was taken away. How else did he return?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. We'll check that. You claim that the Red Berets did not take that bus away?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: There were no Red Berets there. When I passed there -- well, I mean, before me -- this happened before me, perhaps 10 minutes before I wanted to go up there. And then when I got up there in that van, I found Lazar up there, and I heard what he said had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us see how you explained your trip in your amalgamated statement. You say that you were going to work on the 4th of April; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Well, probably. I mean, all of these dates. Was it the 4th or whatever? Probably. Well, if that's what I said in my statement, that is this latest statement. But, I mean, after all these years and all these dates --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It was a Sunday, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was a Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Please, let us just pause between question and answer. In your statement of the 15th of May of 1993 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We did not catch the number of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say it was a Sunday, and on that year, Sunday was on the 5th of April?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: I don't know that either. You probably checked that. I don't know. I know it was a Sunday, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On the 14th of July, 1995, that is 1D3679 - you stated that you took a truck to Pale. You didn't take your own vehicle or the van of Omnipresa [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: I don't know. It was a van, or a truck, or whatever. What did I say? You know, it was the van that took the press around before the war. I don't know, for me, perhaps it was a truck. How do I know? It was a van, or a truck, or whatever. As if that mattered, a truck or whatever, a van.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm going to read it out to you: "I went to work. However, roadblocks had already started and buses were not running. A friend came along, and somehow I managed to get to Pale on this truck. On that day, the communications were down, because for two days --" I cannot see this, but never mind. So some man came on a truck, your friend, you took the truck. So we have three versions, and we have to establish which one was right. One is in your own car, that you were checked and they let you go, the second version is the van for distributing newspapers, and the third one is a truck owned by your friend?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: The van that distributes newspapers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 8 of your amalgamated statement, you say that Braco Paradzina came to you and told you to get lost until the situation calmed down. When did that happen?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: When I was in Pale and I was working, and he came in some car. And he entered the office -- well, he didn't put it that way. He said that I had to go from there because there was no room for Muslims there. Next time, if I come and I find you here, I'll kill you, that's what he said to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Aha, thank you. Is that what you stated in your previous statements?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Maybe I didn't and maybe I didn't. I don't know, I cannot say now. I've given hundreds of statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is what paragraph 8 says: "On the 7th of April, 1992, Braco Paradzina --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a moment. Show him the document. Yes, para 8. Proceed, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we have two versions in Serbian. Can we have the English version for the other participants.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is what it says: "On the 7th of April, 1992, Braco Paradzina came to the Centrotrans workshop and told me to get lost until the situation calms down, so I decided to go ..." And so on and so forth. And let us have a look at what you stated in 1992, probably after the exchange. 1D375. On the 9th of April, 1992, in Centrotrans, Braco Paradzina came and told me to get lost until the situation calms down, so I decided to go to Renovica." And on the 15th of May, 1993 - 1D3677 - you stated something different. You say: "An armed man in camouflage uniform, Braco Paradzina, entered my office, and I knew him from earlier on just by sight."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Can the witness be given an opportunity to see the statements that Mr. Karadzic is referring to? If it helps, the witness has hard copies of the statements in front of him, and in chronological order. He may want to refer to those instead of the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you have them? I wonder whether we have all the photocopies of those statements. But when you refer to the statement in such a manner, it's very difficult for the witness to follow. I would like you to show the passage to the witness. Where can we find that passage in this document?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll find it now. If there's a hard copy, that would be a good thing, if the witness had his own statements in our language, and we can have the English versions on the screen. The first page, lines 13 through 15.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can we zoom in further on the upper part? I see "Paradzina" there, "Braco." Did you find the passage, Mr. Karic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I haven't found it. But all of these statements that Karadzic is referring to were just being supplemented. In some places, I gave more extensive information, in other places, less extensive, but all of them are correct. I couldn't say, word for word, exactly the same thing every time. It's not that I added this, to get lost, that there was no place for Muslims there, and that he walked in with a pistol. All of this is correct, but I was just adding things to my statements as I gave them. But they're all correct. It's true that he came, that he came in uniform, that he was armed, that he told me to get lost, that there was no business for Muslims to be there. All of that is correct. And perhaps every statement is different. It's not that they're incorrect. Maybe I just provided more information and things like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Your next question, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the statement from 1992, you said that he had said to you to get lost until the situation calmed down, and you decided to go to Renovica. And in the statement from the 15th of May, 1993, you stated - that's the one that we have here - that he said to you to get lost because, There is no room for Muslims here anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He answered the question. Move on to your next topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So then you sought shelter in Renovica, and you say that Momcilo Antonic helped you, took you there. That is paragraph 8 of the amalgamated statement: "I went to Renovica to Muharem Alispahic, my father-in-law."

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Muharem Salispahic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I apologise: "I passed by the Serb police roadblocks towards Praca with the assistance of my colleague Momcilo Antonic." This road from Praca to Renovica was under whose control?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Muslim control.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This Momcilo Antonic who helped you pass through Serb territory was a Serb; right?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'm saying this for the benefit of the participants, who cannot distinguish among our names, so please bear with us. And then in the statement of 1993 that was on the screen a moment ago, you say that: "Then one of my colleagues, Momcilo Antonic, a driver, told me that he would take me wherever I wanted to go, but that I should not tell anyone about it. I said to him that he should drive me to Renovica, which is exactly what he did. And we went to Praca. That's how far the Serb roadblocks were. And then from Praca, a Muslim driver took me to Renovica." Does that mean that the driver changed and that a Muslim continued?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Well, because of his own safety. He said, I'll take you to Renovica, if you want, but I'm afraid that they would arrest me there; the Muslims, I mean. Well, that was it. So Sefkija took me to Renovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When did you go to Renovica?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know what the date was. I can't remember. It was immediately after Paradzina. Was it the same day, was it the next day? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In 1992, you said it was on the 9th of April. 1993, that it was on the 7th of April. And, in 1994, on the 9th of April. And in this amalgamated statement, you say the 7th of April; right?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Well, it's most probably the 7th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As for the length of your stay in Renovica, you referred to different periods. How long did you stay in Renovica?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I can't remember. A few days, until the bus came to Renovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Until normal traffic was established; right?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And when was normal traffic established?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. I've just said. A few days afterwards; I don't know. Perhaps the 15th. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. May I remind you, then, that in 1992, you said you stayed seven days. In May 1993, you said that you returned on the 12th of April to Pale. In 1994, you said that you were in Renovica for three or four days, or perhaps five or six days.

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: It's all the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In 1995, in the statement we mentioned, you said that you returned around the 15th of April, 2002, you said the 14th of April, and in this amalgamated statement, paragraph 9, you say that you returned on the 15th of April; right?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: I don't know what all these dates mean for you. Whether it's a day, or two, or three, or five, give or take, I mean, you keep sticking to these dates. That is pointless. I don't see any reason for you to insist on that and to ask me about that, in general.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. How did you return to Pale?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: The first bus came, and I took that first bus to Pale to work there, because they were sending messages that I should go to work, to start working, and then I decided to go to work there. Everything I believed, well, it would have been better had I not believed all that, but there you go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Oh, somebody was sending you messages. Could you tell us why that happened? How come they called you, who called you?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Well, those people living up in Pale, Danilo and Klisara, Zeljko, and Tanic, Milorad, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: These names you mentioned, they're all Serbs, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: I really don't know. I guess they all are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What else could they be?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Nothing. Serbs; there you go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your statement of 1992, you say that you stayed for seven days, and then when buses started running again, you went back and you worked, all the way up until the 22nd of May, 1992, as you stayed with Enver Karic, your uncle. However, in your statement of the 15th of May, 1993, you say that they sent two policemen to get you; right?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Well, they did send two policemen; not on the 15th and not on the 22nd, but on the 28th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The arrest is a different matter. Here, it says that on the 15th of May, 1993, you say: "I was in Renovica until the 12th of April, when two unknown policemen came to my house. They were from the Pale SUP, and they said that they guaranteed my security and safety, and that I should go to work at the Centrotrans office in Pale." Right?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement of 1995 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's time to take a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Just briefly before the break, Mr. President, can we have an indication, if possible, whether the next witness may be required today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't think so. Even according to the little bit of time you've given me, there would be no time for another witness. And I'm hoping for an extension of time, that you would extend my time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: After the break, I expect you to lead us to some important points. We'll have a break. Given the accused's response -- I won't go there, so we'll leave it there. And we'll have a break for half an hour and resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. If we could briefly move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So let's bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, did you perhaps want to hear my reasons for additional time, as you announced?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please go on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The current witness is a witness and participant in very important events at a very important location. The Prosecution has probably the ambition of presenting him as part of a pattern of events in a municipality and in a prison facility. This witness made a couple of statements that are inconsistent in certain elements.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. I would prefer to hear that in the absence of the witness. Mr. Karic, I apologise for your inconvenience. There's still further matters to discuss in your absence. Could you excuse yourself once again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Carry on, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. He's made a couple of statements that are inconsistent in certain important points. They are also inconsistent with testimony of another witness from the same municipality, Witness Sankar [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter is unsure of the name.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence can contest and prove the inaccuracy of a number of points the witness made in his statements. However, what we need for that is time. This is the basis on which we seek additional time, to shed light on a number of points and to challenge all the points that need challenging.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, at the moment the Chamber is of the view that two hours is more than sufficient to cover anything that you refer to, so I would advise you to use your time as efficiently as you can. Judge Morrison has some further comments to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Dr. Karadzic, what you've done in cross-examination so far is really, it seems to me, very peripheral. And if there are challenges to go to the heart of the witness's evidence, in terms of limitation of time and, it may be thought, in terms of tactics, it's always better to make your best points first. The second thing is this: that it's an impermissible line of cross-examination to put what another witness has said by way of inconsistency, and it's something that a witness really can't deal with unless they were sitting in court at the time that the witness gave that evidence, which is highly unlikely. So it's a question of focus. You can do it, because I've seen you do it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellencies. Let me just say I'm grateful for the additional time I'm given. However, if I knew in advance that I had this time available to me, I would not rush through the examination. I know that you will make an adequate ruling if I am successful in what I'm doing, but the shortage of time makes me commit errors on my way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Remember that you don't have to cover every point with every witness. Let's bring in the witness, and try to conclude your cross-examination today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you for your understanding, Mr. Karic. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, in order that the participants and the Trial Chamber may be aware of it, can we agree that Renovica has a predominantly Muslim population; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said in some statements of yours that policemen arrived and guaranteed safety, and in others you said that some of your colleagues from your office called you to come back to work a couple of days after you had gone?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was perhaps three, four, or five days later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So what was the case, really? Was it the policemen who came or your colleagues called you?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Make a pause. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My apologies to the interpreters and participants in the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Therefore, a regular public transport was restored to that area quite soon thereafter, and you returned to Pale?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Yes, but it was on the 22nd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Between the 12th of April and the 22nd of May, you continued working; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 9 of the consolidated statement, you say that the revenue produced by all the companies from Pale was siphoned off to the Crisis Staff of the Municipality of Pale. How are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure about the revenue produced by my company, and I heard that the same was true of the other companies at Pale. And I knew about my company, I knew that for a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you, yourself, see these invoices and payments?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Well, there were no invoices or payments to speak of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Muhamed Saceragic, was he the manager of the branch office at Pale or somewhere else?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: He was the CEO in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your 1994 statement, 1D3678, the last paragraph, you say that the manager said to you quite clearly that you should pay salaries to workers and that the rest should be transferred to the account of the Crisis Staff at Pale?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell Their Honours, was Centrotrans a privately-owned or a socially-owned company at the time?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Socially owned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, could I ask you again to put a pause before you start answering. The interpreters have great difficulty following the conversation. Please. Yes, please continue, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say that from the 15th of May -- or, actually, between the 12th of April and the 15th of May, you stayed in your work-place, and from the 15th of May onwards, you were transferred to ticket sales. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Apart from that transfer, you say that there was no mistreatment or harassment?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Well, there was no harassment, but I was exposed to all sorts of -- well, I was working down there with Serbian refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you mean to say that at the time there was a lot more work to be done at the ticket office where you worked?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. There were at least 10 to 15 buses every day leaving in the direction of Cacak. These were Serbian families fleeing the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's make a break between question and answer. That's why I'm pausing? So there were Serbian families which had arrived in Pale from somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Well, there were those who had arrived there from elsewhere and those who were leaving the area, being locals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: These families who arrived there from elsewhere, what was the place they fled?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Grbavica, Hadzici and Pale, of course. These were Serbian families.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You knew the approximate number of refugees at the time. Was it on the rise?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Well, at the time I worked there, some 10 to 15 buses left the area daily in the direction of Belgrade and Cacak up until the 22nd of May. I can't tell you for the later period, because that was the day I stopped working there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was this high number of refugees, for such a small place such as Pale and for your company, was it a large burden?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Well, not really.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your 1995 statement, you say that in addition to ticket sales, you were also charged with maintaining lists of refugees whom you told or ordered that they should go somewhere else. What do you mean, "ordered"? Did you receive instructions from someone, and you had to give them guidance?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Well, there were lines to Belgrade and Cacak, and you would make tickets for these people who wanted to go there. There was no sort of order involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that there was shortage of food at Pale at the time? You, yourself, said that you suffered privations?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Well, that's true. Shops were closed, and there was nothing to be had, so I would ask people to bring foodstuffs from Sokolac because we had a bus line from Sokolac. On one occasion, I went to Sokolac myself to buy foodstuffs. I even had an unpleasant situation there, but, luckily, nothing happened. I was lucky.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 15 of your statement, you say that Serbian soldiers brought food for the Serbs. Do you mean to say here that these were soldiers from Pale who took food to their families?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: I don't know where it was that I said that. I suppose that since there was nothing to be bought at Pale, they had to make do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 15 of your consolidated statement, you say all the shops at Pale were closed, there was no food to be had, and the Serbian soldiers brought food for the Serbs. You meant soldiers bringing food for their families; right?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Well, probably so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you brought any food by the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You say: "Staple foods were brought to me by the Serbian soldiers from our company"?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Serbian drivers.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now look at D19 briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 15, you say that, meanwhile, explosions and shelling could be heard from Sumbulovac, Trebevic and Hresa upon Sarajevo; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Let's look at this. This is a board of the residents of Serb ethnicity of Hresa and Renovica, and they are giving a list of displaced Serbian families from Renovica. I'll read it to make it easier for you: "After the 15th of May, 1992, immediately after the Serbian forces had collected weapons from the members of Muslim forces in the Renovica Local Commune in the military action, the Muslim forces took revenge on the minority Serbian population, killing four people of Serbian ethnicity and destroying a large number of houses and out-buildings. Given the fact that the military and civilian authorities of Pale municipality did not protect the Serbian population of Renovica in any way, these Serbian families were displaced and have found a temporary shelter in other villages of the municipality with a majority Serbian population. They have left behind considerable movable and immovable property ...," et cetera. Do you remember this event?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: No, not specifically. As far as I know, there were two or three Serb households there. There were two or three Serb houses that I knew of up there. What happened to them, did they leave, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When you found refuge in Renovica, where was that? You must have had someone there. Did you have relatives there?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: My mother-in-law, father-in-law, and my brother-in-law with his wife and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you give us their names?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Muharem is my father-in-law. Serifa is my mother-in-law. Now, as for the brothers-in-law, Munib and Taib.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And is there another brother-in-law there?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. He was known as Zecan.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that he was known as Zecan. That's his nickname. What's his name?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was his nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What was his name?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You don't know your brother-in-law's name?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Your wife's brother, and you don't know his name?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you knew that there were a couple of Serbian households in Renovica?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Well, I did go there in my youth, and I speak from experience. I was also a conductor, so I went there. And I know that nobody harmed them in any way, that the Serbian families left of their own accord. That's the extent of what I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What you mean to say is that they left their homes and estates to seek refuge in Serbian villages with other people, without any reason whatsoever?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm just saying that I don't know who they were and how their departure came about. I don't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that a call was issued for illegally-procured weapons to be surrendered?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: I don't know specifically. I heard that calls were made for weapons to be surrendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Up until your arrival in Sarajevo, that's to say between early May and late -- early April and late May, you were at Pale; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know if a police patrol went to Renovica to collect weapons and that two policemen were killed in an ambush?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: This was on the 22nd of May. That morning, an entire military company, three trucks -- it was early in the morning, at about 6.00, as I was in the ticket box selling tickets. There were at least 100 soldiers went past, and it was then that the incident took place. I heard about it. I heard that two Serbian soldiers were killed and there were wounded Muslims. And as a result, these individuals were brought to the camp in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, please don't mind the fact that we have to be precise. Is it correct that before this action that you described of the 22nd of May, a small patrol set off, and two policemen from that small patrol were killed by Muslims in Renovica; yes or no? Just go ahead and say it.

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know anything about it. I don't know if this is how they set off and if anything like that actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. We will come back to the 22nd of May. In paragraph 16, you say that there were two special units in Pale. How could you tell that these were special units?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Well, I knew them from before. I knew Knezevic very well, I knew Rajko Kusic also. And when I was selling tickets when I was working down there, I would see them. They called them Specials. They wore caps, multi-coloured uniforms. They walked around Pale like some gang. They did whatever they want. When I was detained, they came 'round and they created the most problems, committed killings, beatings, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Are you trying to say that this was a police and a military unit or these were some units that were not part of the general forces?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: I don't know. These were units -- how can I describe them? They were special units, that sort of units. They could do whatever they wanted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it Rajko Kusic, not from Rogatica, but the one from Pale, who was a well-known athlete, karate specialist and a policeman?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: It was Rajko Kusic who was from --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter did not hear where he was from.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was the one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that he was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. The interpreters didn't hear where that Rajko Kusic was from.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From Korani. Actually, it's an area of Pale by the name of Koran.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And you say that you know that he was a member of the SDS. Do you know that he was a policeman? And how do you know that he was a member of the SDS when you said that you did not see him with other members of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Well, how should I know if he was in the SDS or not. He probably was. The SDS party was a popular one, and since he was in a special unit, he must have been a member of the SDS. This is normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know any SDA members at Pale? Was there an SDA branch in Pale?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Since I wasn't a member of any party, I didn't know anyone who was in the SDA or in any party. I wasn't really interested in that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So you were more familiar with the SDS membership than with the SDA membership?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic. I am saying that most probably they were members of the SDS. They wouldn't have been there at all had they not been members of the SDS. The SDS was there, people were members of the SDS. One knows what happened later with the SDS.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic please repeat his question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear your question. Please repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you know that there was a very strong SDA organisation in Pale and that well-known members of the SDA from Pale, Serif Becic, Munir Radaca and Kemo Hrvo, already in 1991, took part in the formation of the Patriotic League?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that. I didn't live in Pale. I lived in Sarajevo. I only worked in Pale. I really didn't have too much time to speak about that or ask about it. I wasn't really interested in that. I only worked in Pale and lived in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: I lived in Sarajevo; I worked in Pale.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But obviously you were interested in the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: I wasn't interested, but I just happened to be familiar with them to know them, and it would have been better had I not.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please look at 1D3733.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the letterhead of the Muslim magazine "Preporod," "Rebirth"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at page 2 in the Serbian. Could we zoom in a little bit more on the left two-thirds. You don't need to zoom in on the whole text.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Allow me to read to you, briefly, the second sentence from the beginning: "The first staff of the Patriotic League of Bosnia-Herzegovina was formed in the mosque in Soukbunar precisely on this day, the 31st of March, 1991, and was made up of Serif Besic, Radaca and Kemo Hrvo from Pale. And you didn't hear of this, not even that this was formed, and you didn't hear of these prominent Muslims from Pale?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know why you're showing this to me at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: With all due respect, Mr. Karic, I'm not accusing you of anything. I'm just trying to see what it is that you know and whether what you know is objective and balanced.

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Well, that, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this being accepted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No basis for us to admit this at the moment. We'll not admit this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that all the villages -- actually, all Muslim villages handed over illegal weapons, except Renovica? You know that?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 17 of your amalgamated statement, you say that 200 to 300 soldiers, led by Malko Koroman, went in the direction of Renovica with one bus, two trucks, and three Pragas, and at 7.00 in the morning. And this is paragraph 17. Today, you said it was 100 soldiers or 100 policemen. How do you know all of this?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Well, more or less, just judging how many people can fit into a bus, into a truck, and how much the Pragas take up. Perhaps it was not 100, 150. Maybe it was 200, 250. There were many, many of them on the bus, around the bus, on the platform, on the roof. They were all over. I saw it with my own eyes as they passed by. I don't know if it was a hundred, 200, 250. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you saw that. Did Malko Koroman command the army or the police?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, he was in command of the police, but at the time, who knows who was in command of what?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Karic, with all due respect, it's important to the Trial Chamber to see if the military or the police embarked on the campaign to disarm the civilians. Malko Koroman was in charge of the police station, not the army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Well, as far as I could see, they were both soldiers and policemen. I don't know who commanded them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How could you tell the police and the military apart?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Well, the military, they had camouflage uniforms, and the police wore thick, dark blue uniforms. It was the police reserves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And it was only by that? You didn't know what military unit it was, did you?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Perhaps they were policemen as well, but they were not wearing blue uniforms, is it?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't like that. I think it was half police and half soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Which army? Which army was that, Mr. Karic?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: The Serbian military.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your statement from 1992, you said that you heard, but today you say that you saw?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: What?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, 1D3675 is where you say, page 2-5: "As I heard, assisted by three Pragas, they left with the intention of disarming Muslims from Renovica, and that is when fighting broke out." Is that correct, "as I heard"?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: No, it wasn't "as I heard," but it was as I saw with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In this statement, it says "as I heard." Let's go to item 5: "Assisted by five Pragas, they left with the intention of disarming Muslims from Renovica, and that is when the conflict broke out. That day, they captured 28 Muslims from Renovica and brought them to the sports hall at Pale." This was the 22nd of May; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your statement from 1994, 1D3678, you mentioned that 500 soldiers went to disarm Muslims?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: You are again --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You do not mention Lazar Bojat, to whom we will come back. Well, let me read to you that paragraph. Here also, you heard, is that correct? And now we're going to read that: "That day, on the --"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly ask for the reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We are not hearing any interpretation. You need to give a reference to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is 1D3678, page 2, paragraph 3, line 10: "That day ..." At the beginning of the line, it says: "22nd of May ..." Line 10 in the third paragraph: "On that day, 22nd of May, 1992, I saw Malko Koroman, the Pale Police Station commander, on a military personnel carrier, followed by about 500 men in military uniform, and I heard that they also had three Pragas. I was told that special forces members Rajko Kusic and so on, were with Koroman then."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see that paragraph?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: No, I don't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, you can look at the cursor. That will show you where it is: "That day ..." Can you see the place where the cursor is?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see it. Well, I was just telling you about the numbers, 200, 300, 500. There were many, many. I don't know how many, but there were many soldiers compared to the number of the Renovica inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: But here you say that you heard from the local inhabitants, and you say that you heard that they had Pragas?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: Well, no, it wasn't the inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: All right. It does say "inhabitants," "locals." That's what it says. All right, well, let's go back to the statement where you talk about Lazar Bojat. This is 1993 now.

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: What 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, all right. 1D3676.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYDEN
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt, Mr. President. Assuming these other statements are not going to be admitted into evidence, I just note the accused's characterisation of what the witness said in this is misleading. He does state that he saw the men, and it's only referring to the three Pragas that he heard that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that has been noted. Thank you, Mr. Hayden.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In this paragraph, the statement from 1993 - this is also on page 2 - you also say: "The 22nd of May, since we were all interested to find out what all this was about, Lazar Bojat, the Centrotrans driver, said that they were going to slaughter the few Muslims in Renovica, and that they would come back quickly in the column moving towards Renovica, there were three Pragas, two trucks, and a bus," and so on and so forth. So in your statement, you say that they set out to disarm the Muslims, and here you are quoting, and in other statements you do not; you quote Lazar Bojat saying that they were going to go and slaughter Muslims?

utterances.speaker: HAJRUDIN KARIC
utterances.text: When I was selling tickets, Lazar was standing in front of the ticket office. There were a lot of people waiting to buy tickets. They were travelling to Belgrade, Cacak. I mentioned that before. Then when these Pragas came by and those soldiers, there was a lot of noise. It was thundering like it was shooting. Somebody said, What is this? And he said, Well, they're just going off to slaughter some Muslims, and they'll be back soon. It was a kind of off-the-cuff remark. He was not with the soldiers. He was at his work-place, driving the refugees. And it was only because I heard from him that I knew where they were going and what they were meaning to do.
